cards.b: Described in words (categories), not numbers, e.g. eye colour, favourite sport.
Numerical data. Can be discrete or continuous.
Discrete: only particular values, often counted (goals, shoe size). Continuous: any value in a range, measured (time, mass, length).
No. Shoe size is discrete. Decimals do not make data continuous.
Primary: collected by you for your purpose. Secondary: already collected by someone else (e.g. census tables).

cards.f: Advantage and disadvantage of secondary data
cards.b: Cheap and quick, often large data sets. But may be out of date, not exactly what you need, or accuracy unknown.
Two variables recorded for each item, e.g. height and arm span of each student.
Census: every member of the population (accurate but costly and slow). Sample: a part of the population (cheaper but may be biased).
A list of all the members of the population from which the sample is chosen, e.g. the school register.
A sample that does not fairly represent the population, because some members are more likely to be chosen.

cards.f: How to take a simple random sample
cards.b: Number everyone in the sampling frame, pick numbers with a random number generator, ignore repeats.

cards.f: How to take a systematic sample
cards.b: k = population ÷ sample size. Choose a random start between 1 and k, then take every kth member.

cards.f: Stratified sample size for a group
cards.b: (group size ÷ population size) × total sample size. Round and check the totals add to the sample size.
Interviewer is told how many of each type to ask and chooses them. Quick, no frame needed, but not random so may be biased.
Overlapping boxes (0–1, 1–2) and not exhaustive (no box for 'more than 5'). Also give a time frame, e.g. per week.

short.q: State one advantage and one disadvantage of carrying out a census. [2]
short.model: Advantage: it is accurate/complete as every member is included. Disadvantage: it is expensive and time-consuming (or impossible if testing destroys the items).
points: disadvantage: costly / slow / impractical for large populations

short.q: A school has 250 students in Year 10, 200 in Year 11 and 150 in Year 12. A stratified sample of 60 is taken by year group. Calculate the number from each year. [3]
Describe how to take a systematic sample of 30 students from a register of 450. [3]
short.model: 450 ÷ 30 = 15. Pick a random starting number between 1 and 15, then take every 15th student on the register after it.

short.q: A questionnaire asks: 'How old are you? 0–20, 20–40, 40–60'. Give two criticisms of the response boxes. [2]
short.model: The boxes overlap (20 and 40 fit two boxes), and there is no box for people over 60, so they are not exhaustive.
points: no box for over 60 / not exhaustive

short.q: A postal questionnaire is sent to 500 customers. Explain why the results may be biased. [2]
short.model: Postal questionnaires often have a low response rate, and the people who reply may have stronger views than those who do not, so the sample is not representative.
points: responders not representative of all customers
